content.content: 1	Large Language Model (LLM) evaluation results vary across reproductions, but variance sources interact, and their relative importance shifts with the benchmark format. We apply Generalizability theory (G-theory) in a fully crossed design with up to seven facets across open-weight instruction-tuned models and five benchmarks. Under binary correctness scoring, a recommended 3-prompt $\times$ 3-seed design achieves $G \geq 0.80$ with 178 items---a 3.1$\times$ item reduction over single-condition designs at the cost of 2.9$\times$ more evaluations per item---a tradeoff that favors multi-facet designs when item construction is costly. Variance decomposition reveals that models differ primarily in which items they find difficult rather than in overall ability, and that the variance structure shifts qualitatively between multiple-choice and free-form benchmarks. Preliminary validation across model scales and architecture families confirms structural stability. We release an open-source G-theory pipeline and D-study budget calculator for evaluation design optimization.
